# KV Cache: A Technical Overview

## What Is KV Cache?

KV cache is a memory optimization technique used in transformer-based language models during autoregressive generation. The name refers to the key-value pairs stored in cache memory—specifically, the attention keys and values extracted from previous tokens in a sequence.

When a model processes text token by token, each token's representation must pass through self-attention layers. In standard inference, recomputing these attention projections for every new token would require reprocessing all preceding tokens, creating quadratic computational complexity relative to sequence length. KV cache solves this by storing the computed keys and values once, then appending only the new token's projections to existing cached tensors on each generation step.

## How It Works Technically

During the forward pass of a transformer layer, each input token gets projected into three vectors: queries (Q), keys (K), and values (V). The attention mechanism computes similarity scores between queries and keys, then uses those weights to aggregate value information. For token position *i*, the K and V matrices depend only on tokens 0 through *i*—they don't change as subsequent tokens are generated.

KV cache exploits this property by caching the accumulated K and V matrices after each token is processed. When generating token *i+1*, the model retrieves the cached K/V from positions 0 through *i*, concatenates them with the newly computed projections for token *i*, and performs attention against this combined set. This reduces per-token computation from O(n×d) to O(d) where n is context length and d is hidden dimension size.

Modern implementations store KV caches either on CPU host memory or high-bandwidth GPU memory depending on size constraints. Techniques

# KV Cache: Enabling Efficient Long-Context Inference

## What It Is

In transformer-based language models, inference proceeds autoregressively—generating one token at a time, with each new token attending to all previous tokens. For every generation step, the model must compute attention scores between the current token and all preceding tokens. The **KV cache** stores the precomputed key and value matrices from prior tokens, eliminating redundant recomputation during sequential generation.

When processing a sequence, the attention mechanism projects each token's embedding into query (Q), key (K), and value (V) vectors. During training, these are computed simultaneously across all positions. During autoregressive inference, however, only one new token is generated per forward pass. Without caching, the model would need to recalculate K and V for *all* previous tokens at every single step—a quadratic waste that makes long sequences computationally prohibitive.

## Why It Matters for Long Context

As context length grows, the KV cache becomes critical for three reasons. First, it transforms the attention computation from O(n²) recomputation per token to O(n) incremental update, reducing memory bandwidth demands dramatically. Second, it enables practical inference times by avoiding redundant matrix multiplications across previously processed tokens. Third, it allows the model to actually leverage long上下文—without caching, the computational cost of attending to thousands of past tokens would make such queries infeasible.

Modern systems optimize KV cache through techniques like paged attention (vLLM), continuous batching, and speculative decoding. Some architectures
